INLA-style posterior approximation for any log-posterior

Source: R/inla-vanilla.R
inla_vanilla.Rd

Approximates the posterior of a parameter vector from its log density alone, using the approximation pipeline of INLAvaan (Jamil & Rue, 2026a, 2026b) with no latent field and nothing model-specific. The pipeline has four stages:

  1. Joint Gaussian (Laplace). The posterior mode \(\vartheta^*\) and the inverse Hessian \(\Omega\) there give a Gaussian approximation \(N(\vartheta^*, \Omega)\) and the Laplace estimate of the log marginal likelihood.

  2. VB mean correction. The Gaussian is recentred at \(\tilde\vartheta = \vartheta^* + \hat\delta\), the mean that maximises its expected log-posterior, with the covariance unchanged.

  3. Skew-normal marginals. For each parameter, the log-posterior is scanned along the conditional mode path of the Gaussian, corrected for the changing volume of the other parameters, and fitted by a skew-normal \(SN(\hat\xi_j, \hat\omega_j, \hat\alpha_j)\).

  4. Gaussian copula draws. sampling() couples the skew-normal marginals through the correlations of \(\Omega\).

Stages 2 and 3 are optional and independent of each other. vb = FALSE skips the VB correction, which leaves the marginals unchanged (they are scanned around the mode) but gives the Laplace log marginal likelihood. marginals = "gaussian" skips the scans and uses the Gaussian's own marginals \(N(\tilde\vartheta_j, \Omega_{jj})\), centred at the VB mean (or at the mode when vb = FALSE); sampling() then draws from the joint Gaussian. So vb = FALSE, marginals = "gaussian" is the Laplace approximation alone, and marginals = "gaussian" alone is the Laplace approximation with the VB correction.

Usage

inla_vanilla(
  logpost,
  init,
  grad = NULL,
  hess = NULL,
  ...,
  vb = TRUE,
  marginals = c("skewnormal", "gaussian"),
  verbose = FALSE,
  silent = FALSE,
  control = list()
)

Arguments

logpost

A function logpost(theta, ...) returning the log-posterior density (up to a constant) at the named numeric vector theta, on the unconstrained scale. See the section on writing logpost.

init

A named numeric vector of starting values. Its length sets the number of parameters and its names label them; unnamed values are called theta[1], theta[2], ..., and a repeated name is numbered in the same way.

grad

Optional function grad(theta, ...) returning the gradient of logpost as a numeric vector. When NULL (the default), finite differences are used.

hess

Optional function hess(theta, ...) returning the Hessian of logpost, the m x m matrix of its second derivatives (a sparse matrix from the Matrix package, and a number when m = 1, work too). It needs grad. When NULL (the default), finite differences of grad are used.

...

Further arguments passed to logpost, grad and hess, such as the data. As in stats::nlminb(), they come after the gradient and the Hessian, and the arguments after them (vb, marginals, verbose, silent, control) must be given by their full names, so data arguments cannot partially match them. The arguments before them can be matched, as in nlminb(): a data argument named g or gr would be taken as grad, and one named h or he as hess, so give it a longer name.

vb

Logical. Apply the VB mean correction? Default TRUE. It enters the log marginal likelihood, and the skew-normal means are checked against it (see summary.inla_vanilla()).

marginals

The marginal of each parameter: "skewnormal" (the default) fits a skew-normal to a scan of the log-posterior; "gaussian" uses the Gaussian marginal of the Laplace approximation, centred at the VB mean when vb = TRUE, with no scans. Abbreviations such as "skew" and "gauss" work too.

verbose

Logical. Print a full diagnostic of each stage under its progress line? Default FALSE. See the section on output.

silent

Logical. Print nothing at all, and muffle the warnings and messages raised during the fit? Default FALSE. The warnings are still recorded in fit$warnings. Cannot be combined with verbose = TRUE.

control

A list of tuning parameters; see the section on control.

Value

An object of class inla_vanilla, with methods for print(), summary(), plot(), sampling() and diagnostics(). It is a list holding, among other things:

  • summary: the posterior summary table (mean, SD, quantiles, mode).

  • mode, cov: the Laplace mode and covariance.

  • mean_vb: the VB-corrected mean (the mode when vb = FALSE).

  • sn: the skew-normal parameters xi, omega and alpha per parameter (with alpha = 0 for Gaussian marginals).

  • vb, marginals, verbose, silent: the settings the fit used.

  • logml: the log marginal likelihood, and logml_laplace its Laplace part.

  • diagnostics: the checks of each stage, which diagnostics() returns under INLAvaan's names and summary.inla_vanilla() explains. optim holds the return code, message and iterations of stats::nlminb(), the gradient of minus the log-posterior at the mode (grad), the whitened gradient there (grad_mode), and the condition number of the Hessian in posterior-SD units (hess_cond). vb holds the iterations of the VB correction, whether it fell back to stats::nlminb() (fallback), and the Kullback-Leibler divergence of the shift (kld_global); it is NULL when vb = FALSE. marginals is a data frame with a row per parameter: mode_shift_sigma, kld, vb_shift, vb_shift_sigma, nmad, alpha, unscanned_mass, vb_step_sigma, mean_gap, gamma1, tails and ridge_bend, with NA for the checks the fit did not run.

  • scan: the scans the skew-normals were fitted to, for plot(fit, type = "sn_fit"): the grid z in posterior SDs from the mode, the log-posterior at each point (logpost, a column per parameter), and the log scale factor logC of each fit on that grid. It is NULL for Gaussian marginals.

  • warnings: the messages of the warnings raised during the fit, as a character vector of plain text, each message once (empty when there were none). They are recorded whether or not silent is TRUE.

Writing logpost

The approximation works on an unconstrained scale: every parameter must be free to take any real value. Reparameterise anything constrained, for example a standard deviation \(\sigma > 0\) as \(\log\sigma\), a probability as its logit, or a correlation as its Fisher \(z\). Means and regression coefficients need no change.

Return -Inf wherever the density is zero or cannot be evaluated, such as outside the support or where a matrix is not positive definite (NA and NaN count the same). The scans and the VB nodes reach several posterior SDs from the mode, and an error raised there stops the fit.

logpost is then the log density of the parameters you pass. When a prior is stated on the natural scale, include the log-Jacobian of the transformation: with \(\vartheta = \log\sigma\) and a prior \(p(\sigma)\), the prior term is \(\log p(e^\vartheta) + \vartheta\). Leaving it out targets a different posterior, not a worse approximation of the same one, and nothing downstream can detect it.

The choice of parameterisation also sets the quality of the approximation, since each parameter gets its own skew-normal on the scale you choose. Scales on which the posterior is close to Gaussian (log standard deviations, Fisher-\(z\) correlations, logits) work best. Natural-scale or derived quantities are available through sampling(fit, fun = ...).

The log marginal likelihood is an estimate of \(\log p(y)\) only when logpost returns the full \(\log p(y, \vartheta)\), including every normalising constant of the likelihood and the prior. Otherwise it is off by the missing constants.

Accuracy

The skew-normal marginals capture skewness that the Laplace approximation misses, and they are accurate to the extent that a skew-normal fits each marginal (see the diagnostics in summary.inla_vanilla()). Like INLAvaan, each marginal is scanned along a straight line through the mode, and the changing volume of the other parameters enters only to first order. When a parameter's spread depends strongly on another, poorly determined parameter, its marginal comes out too narrow, by a factor that vanishes as O(1/n). Examples are a regression coefficient or a mean when the noise SD is uncertain. For a normal mean with unknown variance the SD is about 11% too small at n = 12, 3% at n = 50, and under 1% at n = 200. The ridge_bend diagnostic of summary.inla_vanilla() flags this narrowing where it predicts about 10% or more.

A skew-normal also cannot follow a tail heavier than a Gaussian's. In a structural equation model with 39 parameters and n = 75, the data could not keep two residual variances away from zero, so on the log scale their posteriors had a long, exponential left tail, set by the prior. Checked against MCMC, those two skew-normal marginals were less than half as wide as the posterior, with the 2.5% quantile about 2 posterior SDs too high; the other 37 were within 7% in SD. On the variance scale, where the tail near zero is compressed, the two were much closer: means 0.2 posterior SDs too high and SDs 10 to 15% too small. INLAvaan's marginals of this model are the same as inlavanilla's: Jamil and Rue (2026a, Section 4.4) find the same miss in the lower tail of a variance near zero, the boundary pile-up that a unimodal skew-normal cannot capture. No check is aimed at this. The ridge_bend diagnostic of summary.inla_vanilla() flagged one of the two (0.44), but the other's ridge bend (0.11) was no larger than that of marginals within 7% in SD, and the tails check, which looks only 4 posterior SDs either side of the mode (the Laplace SDs), missed both.

Gradients and Hessians

grad is optional. Without it, derivatives come from finite differences of logpost, and the number of calls grows with the square of the number of parameters m. The mode and Hessian take about m^2 + 6m calls, and the marginals about m(n_grid + 2m + 5). The VB correction takes at most (m + 1)(m + 2) calls per sweep, over a few sweeps: it needs no derivatives, because Stein's identity gives the expected gradient from values of logpost alone. Its VB mean is then exact when the log-posterior is a polynomial of degree four in whitened coordinates, and up to degree six with grad. On test models it was about 0.01 posterior SDs from exact VB (0.003 with grad), and up to 0.1 on a strongly skewed posterior (0.03 with grad), against a VB error of 0.01 to 0.2 SDs from the posterior mean itself. On the most skewed posteriors the VB correction may then not settle, and the fit says it has not converged (see summary.inla_vanilla()); grad is the remedy.

With grad, every stage is more accurate. The fit is also faster when a gradient call costs about as much as a logpost call, as a hand-written gradient usually does, since it then makes about half as many calls in all. A gradient by automatic differentiation (RTMB, TMB) costs about two, and the fit takes about as long as without one. The VB correction takes at most (m + 1)(m + 2) + 1 gradient calls per sweep, at the same nodes. Beyond a handful of parameters it and the marginals are the slowest stages. vb = FALSE skips the VB correction (and its term in the log marginal likelihood), and the skew-normal marginals do not depend on it; marginals = "gaussian" saves the calls of the scans.

hess is optional too, and needs grad, as in stats::nlminb(). With it, stats::nlminb() takes Newton steps to the mode, the Hessian at the mode is the supplied one, and the volume correction of each skew-normal marginal takes one hess call instead of 2m + 2 grad calls. The VB correction and the scans do not use it. The fit is the one grad alone gives, to the error of its finite differences (about 1e-8, relative), except that the mode is found more precisely, so hess saves time rather than adding accuracy. On test models with an automatic-differentiation Hessian (RTMB) the fits took 13% to 35% less time, the most where the Hessian was sparse.

A supplied grad is checked against finite differences at init, and its Jacobian at the mode is checked for symmetry, with a warning if either check fails. A supplied hess is checked at the mode against central differences of grad, along two directions, with a warning if it does not match. Any R function works for logpost, grad and hess, including compiled code (Rcpp, TMB) and RTMB, which differentiates R code. An RTMB function can return the log-posterior itself, and its obj$fn, obj$gr and obj$he are then passed as they are. For a TMB template that returns the negative log-posterior, pass function(x) -obj$fn(x), function(x) -as.vector(obj$gr(x)) and function(x) -obj$he(x), with init = obj$par; its repeated names (one per element of a parameter vector) are numbered, as beta[1], beta[2], and so on. TMB gives no Hessian for a model with random effects.

Control

control is a list with any of:

  • n_grid: number of grid points per skew-normal scan, spread over \(\pm 4\) posterior SDs (default 21).

  • log_threshold: grid points whose log-posterior falls more than this below the maximum are ignored in the skew-normal fit (default -6).

  • vb_maxit, vb_tol: iteration limit (default 25) and convergence tolerance in posterior SDs (default 1e-3) for the VB correction's fixed-point iteration. A step over 1.5 posterior SDs is cut to 1.5. If two steps in a row are cut, or it has not converged after vb_maxit steps, stats::nlminb() takes over.

  • nlminb: a list of stats::nlminb() controls for the mode search. iter.max and eval.max default to 1000 and 2000, and trace = 1 prints its iterations.

Output

By default each stage prints one line as it finishes, with the time it took, and shows a progress bar while it runs for longer than half a second, or than the option cli.progress_show_after when it is set. In knitr or Quarto documents, where a bar cannot redraw in place, a larger cli.progress_show_after in the setup chunk keeps bars out of the output. Warnings, such as a gradient that does not match logpost, are signalled as usual. A fit whose checks look off, such as a mode that was not reached, ends with one warning that lists them, as INLAvaan's does (see summary.inla_vanilla() and diagnostics()).

verbose = TRUE adds a full diagnostic of the fit, in grey lines under each stage. It reports what the fit computes anyway, with no further calls of logpost or grad:

  • Before the mode search: the parameters, where the derivatives come from, logpost at init, and for a supplied grad its largest relative discrepancy from finite differences there.

  • The mode: the message, iterations and evaluations of stats::nlminb(), and whether it was restarted with the parameters rescaled; the log-posterior at the mode, the whitened gradient there (which decides the restart) and the largest Newton step in posterior SDs (which the fit-time warning checks); how the Hessian was taken (and, for a supplied grad, the asymmetry of its Jacobian, or, for a supplied hess, how far it is from central differences of grad); the largest posterior correlation and the smallest eigenvalue of the correlation matrix, which is near zero when some combination of the parameters is poorly identified, and the condition number of the Hessian in posterior-SD units; and the Laplace log marginal likelihood.

  • The VB correction: the largest step, in posterior SDs, at each fixed-point iteration, whether Anderson acceleration or the fallback optimiser was used (and, after the fallback, the step still to go where it landed, and whether it was rerun from there), the largest shift, and the term it adds to the log marginal likelihood.

  • The marginals: the shape, NMAD, ridge bend, tails, unscanned mass and volume correction gamma1 of each parameter, with the values that summary.inla_vanilla() flags marked.

  • The calls of logpost, grad and hess in each stage, and in all, with the total time.

For the iteration trace of stats::nlminb() itself, pass control = list(nlminb = list(trace = 1)).

silent = TRUE prints nothing, for simulations and other repeated fits: no progress bars and no stage lines, and every warning and message raised during the fit, including those of logpost, grad and hess, is muffled. Errors are still raised. Output printed with cat() or print(), by logpost, grad, hess or the trace of stats::nlminb(), is not captured.

Whatever the level, the warnings raised during the fit are recorded in fit$warnings, so that a simulation can check them afterwards.

References

Jamil, H., & Rue, H. (2026a). Approximate Bayesian inference for structural equation models using integrated nested Laplace approximations (arXiv:2603.25690 [stat.ME]). arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.25690

Jamil, H., & Rue, H. (2026b). Implementation and workflows for INLA-based approximate Bayesian structural equation modelling (arXiv:2604.00671 [stat.CO]). arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2604.00671

See also

sampling() for posterior draws and derived quantities, summary.inla_vanilla() and diagnostics() for diagnostics.

Examples

# Normal data with unknown mean and standard deviation, on the scale
# (mu, log sigma)
set.seed(1)
y <- rnorm(30, mean = 5, sd = 2)

logpost <- function(theta, y) {
  mu <- theta[["mu"]]
  sigma <- exp(theta[["log_sigma"]])
  sum(dnorm(y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE)) +
    dnorm(mu, 0, 10, log = TRUE) + # prior on mu
    dexp(sigma, rate = 1, log = TRUE) + # prior on sigma ...
    theta[["log_sigma"]] # ... and its Jacobian
}

fit <- inla_vanilla(logpost, init = c(mu = 0, log_sigma = 0), y = y)
#> ✔ Found the posterior mode in 10 iterations [2ms]
#> ✔ VB mean correction, max shift 0.24σ [1ms]
#> ✔ Fitted 2 skew-normal marginals [3ms]
fit
#> ── INLAvanilla ───────────────────────────────────────── Skew-normal + VB ──
#> 
#> Log marginal likelihood: -66.38 · Converged in 10 iterations (11ms)
#> 
#>               Mean     SD   2.5%    50%  97.5%   Mode
#> 1 mu         5.159  0.327  4.517  5.159  5.800  5.159
#> 2 log_sigma  0.616  0.129  0.377  0.610  0.885  0.599

# The posterior of sigma itself, through the draws
sigma <- sampling(fit, fun = function(theta) exp(theta[["log_sigma"]]))
quantile(sigma, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
#>     2.5%      50%    97.5% 
#> 1.444354 1.832695 2.455869 

# A full diagnostic of each stage
fit <- inla_vanilla(
  logpost,
  init = c(mu = 0, log_sigma = 0),
  y = y,
  verbose = TRUE
)
#> ℹ 2 parameters: mu and log_sigma
#>   Derivatives by finite differences of logpost
#>   logpost at init -481.47
#> ✔ Found the posterior mode in 10 iterations [1ms]
#>   nlminb: relative convergence (4), after 10 iterations (14 function and 26
#>     gradient evaluations)
#>   logpost at the mode -65.06, whitened gradient 9e-08σ, Newton step 9e-08σ
#>     (warning > 0.1σ)
#>   Hessian by second differences of logpost: 6 calls, and 12 more to set the
#>     steps
#>   Posterior correlation matrix: largest correlation -0.0042 (mu,
#>     log_sigma), smallest eigenvalue 1
#>   Hessian condition number 1, in SD units (warning > 1e+08)
#>   Laplace log marginal likelihood -66.41
#>   63 logpost calls
#> ✔ VB mean correction, max shift 0.24σ [1ms]
#>   Fixed-point steps, largest over the parameters (σ): 0.25, 0.0079, 2.3e-04
#>   Converged in 3 iterations, Anderson acceleration at 1 of them; no fallback
#>   Largest shift 0.24σ, for log_sigma (warning > 1σ)
#>   KL term 0.029, giving a log marginal likelihood of -66.38
#>   18 logpost calls
#> ✔ Fitted 2 skew-normal marginals [4ms]
#>              Shape     NMAD  Ridge bend  Tails  Unscanned    gamma1
#>   mu         -0.25  4.2e-05        0.13     ok    6.4e-05  -0.00014
#>   log_sigma   1.32   0.0076     5.5e-06     ok    0.00057      0.13
#>   ! marks what summary() flags: NMAD > 0.1, ridge bend > 0.25, heavy tails,
#>     unscanned mass > 0.05
#>   66 logpost calls
#> ℹ Done: 147 logpost calls in 14ms

# Nothing printed, as in a simulation; any warnings are kept in the fit
fit <- inla_vanilla(
  logpost,
  init = c(mu = 0, log_sigma = 0),
  y = y,
  silent = TRUE
)
fit$warnings
#> character(0)
